items.title: Cut One AI Cost and Two More Grow Back
items.author: Demetrios
items.content:
What does AI really cost once thousands of people inside a company start using it? , Director of AI at Prosus, has been running agents in production since 2024. We put that question to him on a tandem bike ride from a favorite Amsterdam cafe to Vondelpark.

Ioannis explains the decision to stop relying purely on cloud APIs, and why that approach breaks down at the scale of a large company. He covers why agent harnesses and sandboxes are as greedy as software gets, and why agents scheduled to run every five minutes repeat a lesson the data world already learned about freshness. He also explains how the habit of throwing away a codebase and prompting again quietly adds up. His bigger point is that even if model progress froze tomorrow, there would still be about two years of value left to squeeze out. The cheapest wins come from controlling context and running a basic model router, while ten new features a month keep sprouting like Hydra heads.

From there we get into when fine-tuning small models pays off for repetitive work like data analytics, and the eval suites that come as a byproduct of building in-house. Ioannis explains how owning the stack let Prosus grow a GPT-3 Slack bot into a full agent harness. He also explains why committing to a single vendor or open source project is a bigger bet than it looks, and how to balance top-down priorities with bottom-up building across the company. We close on hiring. Ioannis looks for system design over syntax, a nose for the over-engineered code AI models love to produce, and enough agent intuition to know when to build something yourself and when to let the agent decide.

items.title: SED News: PHP’s Megabug, a Hidden Mic at OpenAI, and Dead AI Products
items.content:
SED News is a monthly podcast from Software Engineering Daily where hosts Gregor Vand and Sean Falconer break down the biggest stories shaping software engineering, Silicon Valley, and the broader tech industry.

In this episode, Gregor and Sean cover the PHP remote code execution flaw that hit an estimated 70 percent of the internet, the recording device an OpenAI employee hid in a conference room, and a busy run of deals including Chroma joining Replit, Cloudflare taking Deno, and Supabase acquiring Turso.

The main topic tours the AI graveyard, sorting recent product failures into patterns: features swallowed by bigger platforms, runaway hits too costly or risky to sustain, interfaces made redundant by agents, and hardware that never materialized.

As always, the episode wraps up with a few standout Hacker News threads, including why washing machines took 50 years to catch on, a location-aware local Wikipedia, and a Figma quirk that traces back to the Windows Numlock key.sponsor@softwareengineeringdaily.com

items.title: Demis Hassabis and the Race to Build AI with Sebastian Mallaby
items.content:
Demis Hassabis founded DeepMind in 2010, before machines could reliably tell a cat from a dog. He believed that artificial general intelligence was achievable, and that it should be built safely and deliberately. Along the way, Hassabis shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for AlphaFold, the system that cracked the fifty-year problem of predicting protein structures. Fifteen years on, the LLM race has erupted across rival labs and countries, and AI has become one of the most consequential and contested technologies of the era.

Sebastian Mallaby is a two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist and a longtime chronicler of the collision between innovation and capital, from hedge funds to central banking to Silicon Valley. His latest book, The Infinity Machine, is a portrait of Hassabis and DeepMind built on more than thirty hours of candid conversation, beginning just as ChatGPT set off the AI frenzy, and drawing as well on Hassabis’s estranged cofounder, his rivals, and academic pioneers who now fear for human survival. Mallaby is also the Paul A. Volcker Senior Fellow for International Economics at the Council on Foreign Relations.

In this episode, Sebastian joins Kevin Ball to talk about Demis Hassabis and the founding of DeepMind, the pioneering breakthroughs that followed, and how the field arrived at the current moment in AI.

items.title: How We Taught Claude Code to Solve Jira Tickets and Address Code Reviews - DevConf.US 2026
items.author: DevConf
items.content:
<article>Speaker(s): Bryan Cox, Alberto Garcia Lamela

What if your backlog could shrink while your team focuses on high-impact features? On the HyperShift team at Red Hat, we built an AI-powered workflow using Claude Code that autonomously picks up Jira tickets, implements solutions, opens PRs, and even responds to peer review feedback — all without a developer lifting a finger.

In this talk, we'll walk through the key automations we built as Claude Code skills, orchestrated through OpenShift CI periodic jobs:

jira:solve — A four-phase pipeline triggered weekly by a periodic CI job. Given a Jira issue, it fetches the ticket details, analyzes the codebase, generates an implementation plan, writes the code and tests, and runs verification (linting, builds, unit tests). Then an AI peer review evaluates the changes for code quality issues. A third phase automatically addresses the review findings and pushes fixes. Only after this internal review cycle completes does the final phase open a PR.

address-reviews — A separate periodic job that runs every three hours. It queries GitHub for agent-created PRs with pending review comments from humans or AI reviewers, categorizes them by priority (blocking, change requests, questions, suggestions), makes the requested code changes, amends the relevant commits, and posts concise replies — closing the feedback loop without context-switching a developer. It can also be triggered on-demand for any PR via a Prow comment.
Together, these create a pipeline where low-priority backlog items flow from Jira to review-ready PRs with minimal human intervention. Developers review the AI's work rather than doing it themselves, acting as supervisors instead of implementers for routine fixes.

We'll cover:

Architecture: How we built a system of Claude Code skills that encode our team's standards — code formatting conventions, Gherkin-style test patterns, effective Go idioms, conventional commit formatting, PR templates, and a project-specific AI review profile — so the AI produces output that meets the same bar as a human contributor.

The solve pipeline: Jira ticket parsing → codebase analysis → plan generation → implementation → verification → AI peer review → review fixes → PR creation

The review loop: How the address-reviews job triages human and AI feedback, makes surgical code changes, amends commits, and replies to reviewers

Guardrails: Comment deduplication, authorization checks, token refresh across long-running phases, and why human review remains essential

Results and lessons learned: What works, what doesn't, and where human judgment is still irreplaceable

Whether you're a platform engineer, SRE, or developer tired of your backlog growing faster than you can triage it, this talk will give you a practical blueprint for putting AI to work on the tasks your team doesn't want to do and the lower-priority ones it doesn't have time to do.

<article>Speaker(s): Aseef Imran, Sana Sharma

As we enter a post-LLM world, we face a critical trade-off: the immediate Efficiency of AI versus the long-term cultivation of human Expertise. While LLMs can execute hours of human labor in minutes, the ""expertise"" an AI builds is fleeting, as it persists only as long as its context window. In contrast, human labor produces a trove of expertise: insights, foresight, and contextual understanding that span a career. When we offload cognition to AI, we risk losing the very ingenuity required to innovate beyond the training data.
While LLMs are a powerful tool, their use carries risks and trade-offs that must be managed. In this talk, we identify three key elements for balancing this trade-off:
* Intention: Choosing when and how to use AI by understanding the cost of personal expertise loss.
* Innovation: Combating LLM-induced stagnation.
* Integrity: Maintaining honesty and trust when claiming ownership of AI-generated work.

Drawing on academic research and real-world industry examples we highlight that while LLMs can mimic the results of expertise, they struggle to replicate the meta-cognition and abstraction required to solve the problems of tomorrow without expert help.

items.title: The Model Is a Commodity. The Harness Is the Product - DevConf.US 2026
items.author: DevConf
items.content:
<article>Speaker(s): Shubhank Saxena

Most conversations about agentic AI start with the wrong question: which model should we use? Models commoditize on a six-month cycle. The team that picked the right model last quarter is one release away from being wrong, and the next release after that. What actually differentiates a production agentic system isn't the model, it's the operational layer around it: tool routing, conversation state, cost controls, guardrails, observability, audit trails. That layer is where the engineering compounds.

This talk is for engineers building agentic systems on real backends, not framework demos, not greenfield AI startups, but the boring middle where most production work lives: a service, an ORM, a queue, a model API. We'll separate durable patterns that survive a model swap from disposable ones you'll delete in six months as models improve, and look at how to design the boundary between them so your stack absorbs capability gains rather than breaking.

The talk has three parts. First, the wrong question, ""which model?"" dominates the conversation, and what the right question looks like. Second, the durable layer-six patterns shown in framework-free Python, each in roughly 30 lines: tool routing, the agentic loop with bounded rounds, conversation compaction that doesn't corrupt tool-call structure, race-free cost tracking, audit-driven observability, and content moderation as fail-open infrastructure. Third, the disposable layer, retry logic, certain guardrails, aggressive compaction; code that's load-bearing today and will be dead weight in two model generations. We'll cover how to detect that a layer has aged out, and how to keep the boundary clean so removal is a deletion, not a rewrite.

What you'll leave with: a working vocabulary for what's durable vs. disposable in your own stack (more useful, in practice, than the SDK / framework/harness distinction); a public gist of framework-free reference patterns to take home; and a diagnostic for spotting the parts of your current system that are about to age out.

What this talk deliberately avoids: framework recommendations or comparisons (this talk is about the layer frameworks abstracted over), live model demos (capability differences across frontier models are not the point), and product case studies. Patterns are presented stack-agnostically; production grounding is implicit, not the spine.

Audience: backend and platform engineers shipping agentic features in production; technical leads making architecture decisions about whether to adopt agent frameworks. Prerequisites: comfort reading Python and basic familiarity with calling an LLM API. No prior agent framework experience required; this talk works equally well for engineers who've never used LangChain and for engineers ripping it out.

<article>Speaker(s): Anass Tissirallah

Building a risk engine means making decisions from information that is rarely complete, clean or perfectly reliable.

The data can come from APIs, databases, documents, public sources, historical events or unstructured text. Some information may be missing, contradictory, outdated or even intentionally misleading.

Adding AI to this process creates new possibilities, but also new engineering challenges. How much should we trust the model? How do we validate its output? And more importantly, how do we explain why the system reached a particular risk decision?

In this talk, I’ll share the engineering patterns behind building a production-grade AI risk engine.

I’ll cover:

• How to design a pipeline that transforms heterogeneous and unstructured data into usable risk signals

• How to combine deterministic rules, traditional data processing and LLMs without making the LLM the source of truth

• How to handle missing, conflicting and suspicious information

• How to use confidence scoring and validation layers around AI generated signals

• How to aggregate multiple signals into an explainable risk decision

• How to make every decision traceable and auditable

• How to evaluate AI components when false positives and false negatives have real consequences

• How to build observability around the whole pipeline so engineers can understand what happened when a decision goes wrong

items.author: DevConf
items.content:
<article>Speaker(s): Aishwarya Ramasethu

Building an agent that calls one tool is straightforward. Building one that orchestrates multiple MCP-connected tools to complete a real task is where things get architecturally interesting and quietly dangerous.

When an agent hands off to an external tool, something subtle happens: control leaves your system. The tool executes, returns a result, and your agent trusts it. Most developers don't think carefully about that moment until something goes wrong like a tool returns unexpected output, an agent takes an action it shouldn't, or a chain of tool calls produces a result nobody intended.

This talk is about the architectural decisions that happen at those handoff points. We'll look at how MCP structures the relationship between agents and tools, where trust gets implicitly granted in ways developers don't notice, and what composing multiple tools together actually looks like when the task is non-trivial.

The demo walks through an agent completing a real multi-step task using several MCP-connected tools, deliberately hitting the failure modes that show up when tool outputs are ambiguous, conflicting, or outside the agent's expected context. We'll look at how to structure tool composition so the agent stays in a predictable, auditable state throughout.

You'll leave with a mental model for reasoning about trust in agentic systems and concrete patterns for composing MCP tools without losing control of what your agent is actually doing.

items.title: Cutting GPU Kernel Autotuning from 20 Minutes to 90 Seconds in Helion - DevConf.US 2026
items.author: DevConf
items.content:
<article>Speaker(s): Alessandro Sangiorgi

Writing high-performance GPU kernels should be a tight developer loop: edit, run, measure, repeat. In Helion, a Python DSL that lowers to Triton, that loop is often dominated by autotuning. Full random search could find excellent kernels, but it often took 10 to 20 minutes per compile. A strategy that starts from a default kernel configuration finished in seconds, but produced kernels 14-31% slower. Worse, the autotune cache was tied too closely to source identity: rename a variable, move code around, or change a comment, and prior tuning work could be lost.

This talk presents `FROM_BEST_AVAILABLE`, a warm-start strategy I contributed to Helion - now the default for quick autotuning - that seeds search from configurations previously tuned for the same input characteristics and device, even when the kernel source has changed. Instead of forcing developers to choose between “slow but good” and “fast but worse,” it reuses prior tuning work to start from a promising neighborhood while still allowing the autotuner to search.

This reduced MatMul autotuning time from 1238 seconds to 92 seconds while matching full-search quality across the seven kernels we benchmarked. I’ll cover how the loose-match key was designed, the trade-offs behind it, and concrete examples of how this approach can improve developer iteration without sacrificing kernel quality.
---

items.title: LLM-Tuna 2.0: Agentic Profiling and Knowledge-Driven Optimization for vLLM - DevConf.US 2026
items.author: DevConf
items.content:
<article>Speaker(s): Thameem Abbas Ibrahim Bathusha, Aanya Sharma

**Are you deploying Large Language Models and struggling to squeeze every ounce of performance out of your costly GPU infrastructure?** While engines like vLLM are industry standards, using their default configurations for your unique complex workload shape \- involving long prefill, extreme sequence lengths, or high concurrency \- can often leave performance on the table. Traditionally, tuning these parameters meant relying on manual tuning or black-box Bayesian Optimization. But what if the tuning could *reason* about why a configuration failed?

This session introduces the next evolution of **llm-tuna**, an open-source framework for automated LLM serving optimization. Building on our research published in the ACM ([link](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3774904.3792953)), we introduce an **agentic feedback loop** where an AI agent manages a persistent Performance Knowledge Base. Instead of just navigating a parameter space, the agent proactively:

1. **Reads and Interprets:** Analyzes vLLM logs and engine metrics to identify memory pressure or compute bottlenecks. 
2. **Profiles and Diagnoses:** Triggers low-level **PyTorch profiling** and kernel-level analysis to understand *why* certain batch sizes or CUDA graph settings underperform. 
3. **Learns and Adapts:** Grows its knowledge base with every experiment, allowing it to bypass inefficient search paths and suggest optimizations that pure statistical models might miss and accelerate the search for newer users of the framework.

We will showcase the architecture—leveraging a kubernetes cluster for distributed, isolated trials—and demonstrate how this ""Expert-in-the-Loop"" approach outperforms standard baselines. This study will show how the progression improves over traditional statistical approaches. Attendees will see real-world case studies on models like **Qwen2.5** and the massive **DeepSeek-R1-671B** on H100/H200 clusters.

### **Key Takeaways:**

* **The Agentic Edge:** How a reasoning agent identifies bottlenecks that Bayesian Optimization ignores. 
* **Closing the Loop:** Integrating PyTorch profiling and log analysis into the automated tuning cycle. 
* **Building a Performance Moat:** Leveraging a persistent, research-backed knowledge base to accelerate deployments across diverse GPU architectures (H100/H200). 
* **Multi-Objective Optimization:** Balancing the trade-offs between prefill latency, decode throughput, and VRAM efficiency.

You are tasked with standing up a large multi-project ecosystem that you are not familiar with. What do you do? Do you find yourself stuck reading pages of documentation, overwhelmed at the idea of understanding and deploying all these new components? Turns out, learning such systems by deploying components one at a time — with an AI partner tracing failures, explaining architecture, and handling mechanical work — can be significantly faster and more effective.

This talk presents a week-long experiment in using AI-assisted collaboration to build a comprehensive understanding of a Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem spanning ~7 different open source projects. The approach followed a deliberate loop: broad question, minimal deploy, let it fail, deep trace with the model to understand why, then scope the next increment. The result is a reproducible reference architecture that stands up a full MCP stack in ~10 minutes — catalog-driven server discovery, lifecycle operator managed deployment, gateway routing, Keycloak identity, per-tool authorization via Kuadrant AuthPolicy, TLS, Vault-backed credential injection, and namespace-isolated multi-tenancy with virtual MCP servers for group-based tool filtering.

Beyond the technical aspects, this talk examines the collaboration pattern itself. AI accelerated breadth — cross-component context, YAML mechanics, integration debugging — while the human supplied direction, skepticism, and architectural judgment: deciding when to push back on over-engineering, when a workaround was acceptable versus when it needed upstreaming, and where to draw the boundary between temporary scaffolding and lasting patterns.

Attendees will come away with practical insights on using AI as a learning partner for complex integration problems and a perspective on how critical thinking changes shape, but doesn't necessarily disappear when AI enters the workflow.

items.title: From Slop Code to Software Factories

Two people, one tandem bike, and a lot of near misses along Amsterdam’s canals. , CEO and co-founder of HumanLayer and the person who coined “context engineering,” climbs on the back to talk about a problem every AI-heavy engineering team eventually hits: code that runs today that nobody understands three months later.

The ride starts with an old joke from the Claude 3.7 days: ship the slop, it’ll be GPT 7’s problem. That joke is aging badly now that GPT 6 is out and still can’t design clean abstractions. From there it becomes a tour of how agents are actually used right now. Computer use checks in for flights and books government appointments. Two hours of raw footage became a rough but promising product demo through Opus 4.8 and the Palmier MCP while Dex was out for a run. And the best MCP tools turn out to be the ones that mirror what Claude Code and Codex were trained to call.

Off the bike, over pour-over coffee, the questions get bigger. Are browser agents a bandaid until everything goes headless? What happens to ad-funded websites and upsells when an agent does the shopping? Why does chat still feel like such a low-bandwidth way to work with models? And why is every principal engineer quietly building their own software factory, then getting buried in the sync, streaming and approval plumbing that HumanLayer wants to turn into building blocks, the way GitHub Actions did for CI?

items.title: AI Regulation and What Every Tech Company Should Know
items.content:
The rapid rise of AI has set off a flurry of legal and regulatory activity. There is no single AI law to follow. Instead, there are overlapping circles of regulation, where privacy, cybersecurity, consumer protection, employment, and IP laws all continue to apply alongside newer AI-specific rules. Europe has its EU AI Act, but the U.S. has no federal equivalent yet. In its place is an emerging patchwork of more than 150 state AI laws, and the picture shifts every few months as new legislation and guidelines arrive. For engineers and tech companies, it can feel impossible to know what applies and where the real risks lie.

Shannon Yavorsky is a data lawyer who co-leads the Cyber, Privacy and Data Innovation group and the AI practice at the international law firm Orrick. She advises companies across sectors from health technology to financial services on how to develop and deploy AI responsibly amid this evolving regulatory environment.

In this episode, Shannon joins Kevin Ball to make sense of that landscape. They discuss how to map the concentric circles of regulation that actually apply to you, the risk spectrum separating a low-stakes manufacturing tool from a high-stakes system making loan or healthcare decisions, the problem of shadow AI and why recorded meetings can become a litigation liability, how to build an AI governance program, and more.sponsor@softwareengineeringdaily.com

items.title: Managing AI Coding Costs at Scale
items.content:
Over the past couple of years, companies raced to get their employees using AI, often encouraging them to lean on it as much as possible. However, as AI coding tools spread through engineering teams, many companies watched their AI bills explode. That kind of runaway cost growth can threaten a business, so the new challenge is capturing the productivity gains from AI without the spending spiraling out of control.

Databricks is a data and AI company that hit this problem early, running AI tools across thousands of its own engineers. Rather than clamp down on usage, the team built a set of practical ways to manage the cost, from taking advantage of steadily falling model prices to automatically routing each request to the cheapest model that can still do the job well.

Patrick Wendell is a co-founder of Databricks, where he leads engineering teams and has driven much of the company’s internal AI adoption. He recently wrote a viral blog post on managing AI coding costs that reached the top of Hacker News. In this episode, Patrick joins Kevin Ball to discuss why AI costs suddenly exploded, the main levers companies have to bring them under control, the trade-offs between managing costs on the server versus in the developer’s tools, and why the next big challenge is giving AI the right context about how a company actually works.sponsor@softwareengineeringdaily.com

items.title: Tim O’Reilly
items.author: Demetrios
items.content:
A large language model knows everything and nothing at the same time. , founder and CEO of O’Reilly Media, joins us ahead of his keynote at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America to talk about what that paradox means for the people building with these models.

We start with what Tim is bringing to the stage in San Jose, then move to the craft of steering a model. The right words work almost like spells that open up new regions of latent space. Something as small as telling a model to use a computer can unlock a new tier of capability, where agents go off and do real work.

From there, the conversation turns philosophical. Tim makes the case for mechanism design: shaping the rules of a system so the outcomes we want become the natural ones. What happens when you give 200 engineers who have barely touched AI a coding assistant and a six-month deadline to rebuild their platform? , a principal engineer who previously led AI enablement at HelloFresh, has done exactly that, and he chose Sonnet over Opus on purpose.

His reasoning is what he calls "Sonnet maxxing." A model that reasons less and stops sooner keeps developers involved, and that matters a lot when the codebase is banking software full of hard business rules. The result was 800,000 lines of code, about 60% of them written by Sonnet, shipped by a team that never stopped thinking for itself. Pep also explains how to justify the spend once the token-maxxing era ends and the CFO starts asking questions. He covers a scatter chart that plots token spend against output, the uncomfortable question of whether a 1% better home screen was worth $20K in tokens, why he measures gains in headcount rather than 2x or 3x multipliers, and where he fell short when trying to prove ROI at HelloFresh.

We also get into a codebase test you can run yourself, why AI recommendations quietly narrow your choices, and multiplayer refinement sessions where the whole team works through the agent's questions together. Pep shares an experiment where designers and engineers got the same one-shot prompt, and it showed how words like "scalable" and "maintainable" steer a model. We finish with how his team built a meta harness on top of Claude Code, after finding that 85% of their code followed the same path: refinement, specification, implementation, verification.

Codebases in enterprise organizations often span hundreds of thousands, or even millions, of lines of code. In many cases, changes must follow established patterns precisely, or risk introducing costly security or operational issues. A common challenge with AI coding tools is that they struggle at this scale: LLM context windows cover only a fraction of a large codebase, and output quality degrades the longer an agent runs.

Blitzy is an autonomous software development platform for the enterprise. It starts by understanding your entire codebase, building a knowledge graph that acts as a shared source of truth. From a well-defined spec that engineers review and approve, it orchestrates specialized agents that work in parallel to build, review, and test code autonomously at scale. The result is a pull request that engineers can then review and merge

Sid Pardeshi is the CTO and co-founder of Blitzy, and he previously worked at NVIDIA. items.title: Physical AI at NVIDIA
items.content:
In recent years, the main impact of AI has been on the digital world, and most notably software engineering. However, its longer-term effect on the physical world may prove even more profound, reshaping how cars drive themselves, how factories run, and how robots move through homes and warehouses.

World models are at the center of the movement to bring AI into the physical space. These models take in observations of the current state of the world and predict what comes next, which lets a robot plan its next move or a car anticipate the road ahead. NVIDIA has been building a family of these models called Cosmos, and sits at the frontier of physical AI and robotics.

Amit Goel has been at NVIDIA for fifteen years, and he is currently the Head of Robotics Ecosystem and Edge AI Product. In this episode, Amit joins Matt Merrill to discuss what separates physical AI from digital AI, how world models plan and predict, the two-tower architecture that lets a robot reason and act at once, why training on video demanded a new data pipeline, and how any developer can start building in this space.

items.title: Software Verification in the Age of Coding Agents
items.content:
Software testing is widely understood as essential to building reliable systems, and it’s one of the hardest things to get right. A fundamental issue is that tests are good at confirming the behavior a team expects, but the most damaging failures tend to hide in the edge cases no one thought to check during development. Those blind spots are only growing as AI produces more code that no human has closely reviewed.

Antithesis is a software verification company built around an approach called deterministic simulation testing. The platform runs a customer’s software in a fully controlled environment, exploring thousands of different paths through it at runtime. Crucially, the paths aren’t pre-specified and they’re not merely the expected cases. In this way, it can surface rare, damaging bugs that normal testing would never catch.

Carl Sverre is on the Red Team at Antithesis and he also leads much of the company’s AI strategy. In this episode, Carl joins Sean Falconer to discuss the Antithesis approach to software verification, why reliability tooling has been chronically underinvested, what makes stateful and distributed systems so hard to test, how deterministic simulation testing works under the hood, and much more.Full Disclosure: This episode is sponsored by Antithesissponsor@softwareengineeringdaily.com

Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project’s community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private.

They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw’s “skills over features” approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam’s case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
